name: Dundee Hills

sheet.soil: Red Jory clay, from volcanic basalt, deep and well drained.
sheet.elevation: ⟦elev|200 to 1,067 feet|61 to 325 m⟧. This vineyard sits near 380.

claims.claim: The Dundee Hills AVA was approved in 2004, as Oregon's eighth AVA.
The name started as a proposed 'Red Hills', for the red soil. The petition was amended to Dundee Hills.
Jory soil covers about 80 percent of the AVA. It is a red, well-drained volcanic clay.
Jory soil formed from weathered Columbia River basalt. The lava flows date to about 15 to 16 million years ago. The soil runs ⟦elev|4 to 6 feet|1.2 to 1.8 m⟧ deep.
The steeper western slopes have Willakenzie soils, a sedimentary soil, rather than Jory.
Vineyards run from the ⟦elev|200 foot|61 meter⟧ contour up to a high point of ⟦elev|1,067 feet|325 m⟧.
Nights are warmer and frost is less likely than on the valley floor. Growing seasons run a little warmer than most Willamette Valley AVAs.
Pinot Noir from Jory is often bright and elegant, with earthy, truffle-like flavors and a silky feel.

terms: American Viticultural Area. A wine labeled with one must take at least 85% of its grapes from that area.
Oregon is stricter than federal law: a wine named for an AVA needs 95% of its grapes from that AVA, and one named for an AVA wholly in Oregon must use only Oregon grapes.

blurb.text: A Willamette Valley AVA in Yamhill County near Newberg, with reddish Jory silt, clay and loam soils. The Chehalem Mountains to the north buffer it from Columbia Gorge air, cold in winter and warm in summer. David Lett planted Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris there in 1966.
